items.desc: In representative democracies, it is important that climate change policies are developed through transparent processes and with citizen representation, which in turn requires an understanding of how climate-related events influence public support for such policies.

items.title: 121-million-year-old fossils suggest Longipteryx had no tail feathers
items.desc: Around 121 million years ago, somewhere in modern northeastern China, an early bird took to the skies. If you drew its silhouette, you'd notice something was missing. Unlike any bird alive today, it had no tail feathers.

items.title: The upside of untidiness: Why a little mess can be good for your home
items.desc: If we're to follow the philosophy of organizer extraordinaire Marie Kondo, a tidy home is a better home.

items.title: Radio images reveal disturbances from Betelgeuse's mysterious companion that lurks within its shadows
items.desc: The well-known star Betelgeuse has a mysterious houseguest—and it's shaking the rafters, rattling the pipes and slamming the cupboards (metaphorically speaking). It's causing enough subtle atmospheric disturbance that it might as well be making ghost noises. Who's to blame? New data suggest that its recently discovered companion star, Siwarha, is the one doing the haunting.

items.title: Technician cracks 1,600-year-old mystery to replicate color-changing effect of Roman glass masterpiece
items.desc: The Lycurgus Cup, a world-renowned 4th-century A.D. artifact housed in the British Museum, is constructed of "dichroic" glass that shifts from jade green in reflected light to ruby red in transmitted light. This means that depending on where the light source is positioned, observers can see the cup displayed in two distinctive, contrasting colors.

items.title: Marine molecule may help combat 'brain-eating' amoeba
items.desc: Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), a parasitic disease that causes the rapid deterioration of brain tissue, is one of the most lethal infections known, with a fatality rate exceeding 97%. Caused by the free-living amoeba Naegleria fowleri (N. fowleri), the disease progresses with devastating speed, often leaving patients with only a few days to respond to treatment.

items.title: The mathematics of growing a shell—recreating diverse mollusk shells with just three inputs
items.desc: Kaushik Bhattacharya is an engineer and materials scientist, but he has always been fascinated by seashells. Part of the draw is the "beautiful" idea that even simple organisms like mollusks can construct wonderfully complex structures over and over again, even in differing environments. He marvels at nature's engineering capabilities.

items.title: See no evil: How willful ignorance supports the illegal tobacco trade
items.desc: Adopting a "don't ask, don't tell" approach to illicit tobacco enables people to avoid thinking about where cheap smokes come from, researchers at the University of Otago, Wellington, have found.

items.title: Anyone Can Dock: Molecular docking platform brings protein-binding predictions to smartphones, tablets and computers
items.desc: A new platform, developed by researchers at the Center for Computational Sciences, University of Tsukuba, in collaboration with Mahidol University, makes molecular docking easier to access, understand, and integrate into experimental research. The work is published in the Journal of Cheminformatics.

items.title: Common drugs may help dangerous viruses spread through the body
items.desc: A surprising discovery reveals that widely used anti-inflammatory drugs may unintentionally help dangerous viruses spread through the body. Scientists found that JAK inhibitors, prescribed for rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory diseases, can weaken a crucial immune defense against influenza, COVID-19, and other infections. By suppressing genes that normally fight viruses, these medications may leave patients more vulnerable to infection.

items.title: James Webb discovers a scorching lava planet with a “giant sunscreen”
items.desc: A scorching lava planet 280 light-years away has surprised astronomers by apparently maintaining a thick atmosphere despite conditions that should have stripped it away billions of years ago. James Webb Space Telescope observations suggest that TOI-561 b reflects about 75% of incoming starlight, possibly because of mineral clouds that act like a giant sunscreen. The planet may also be continually replenishing its atmosphere through gases released from a global ocean of molten rock.

items.title: Smithsonian scientists just recreated the first 2 billion years of the Universe
items.desc: Scientists have created one of the largest and most detailed simulations of the early universe ever made, offering an extraordinary new glimpse into the cosmos shortly after the Big Bang. Called Lumina, the groundbreaking simulation recreates the universe’s first 2 billion years, showing how dark matter, gas, and radiation interacted to give rise to the earliest stars, galaxies, and black holes.

items.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
items.desc: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

items.title: Exercise doesn't just strengthen your heart. It rewires it
items.desc: Regular exercise does more than strengthen the heart. New research reveals that it actually reshapes the nerves controlling how the heart functions, and the changes are surprisingly different on the left and right sides of the body.

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising clue to why some brains resist Alzheimer’s
items.desc: Why do some people stay mentally sharp even when their brains show signs of Alzheimer’s disease? Scientists in the Netherlands may have uncovered an important clue hidden in a rare group of immature brain cells. Researchers discovered that these cells remain present even in people over 80, but their behavior differs dramatically between those who develop dementia and those who remain cognitively healthy.

items.title: A 2,700-year-old solar eclipse just revealed something surprising about Earth
items.desc: A solar eclipse recorded more than 2,700 years ago is revealing surprising secrets about Earth's rotation and the Sun's ancient behavior. By correcting an eight-kilometer error in the location of an ancient Chinese capital, scientists were able to reconstruct a total solar eclipse that occurred in 709 BCE and obtain more accurate measurements of how fast Earth was spinning at the time.

items.title: Scientists solve a 30-year mystery behind inflammatory bowel disease
items.desc: Scientists have identified a hidden cause of inflammatory bowel disease: antibodies that disable the immune system’s natural ability to control inflammation, potentially explaining severe illness in thousands of patients. The breakthrough also solves a 30-year genetic mystery and could pave the way for more precise diagnoses and targeted treatments.

items.title: Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging
items.desc: Mayo Clinic scientists have uncovered surprising new insights into “zombie cells,” aging cells that linger in the body and contribute to inflammation and disease. Seven studies reveal why these cells are harmful and identify new strategies for targeting them, including a natural compound found in tomatoes. In aging mice, experimental treatments reduced inflammation and improved physical and brain health. The findings could open the door to therapies that combat some of the biological processes behind aging.

items.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
items.desc: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

items.title: Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
items.desc: Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices called skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time, revealing new ways to manipulate these unusual structures. The breakthrough could help make brain-like computers a reality, potentially enabling dramatically smaller and more energy-efficient technology.

items.title: Archaeologists may have just found the world's oldest shipwreck
items.desc: A mysterious shipwreck off Turkey’s coast may be the oldest ever discovered, dating back approximately 4,500 years to the age of the Egyptian pyramids. Although the wooden vessel has disappeared, its surviving pottery cargo reveals clues about an ancient trading network that may have connected distant Mediterranean civilizations. Researchers believe the ship may have crashed against rocks during a storm while transporting valuable goods such as oil, wine, or tree resin.

items.title: Chinese scientists discover “D-rex,” a giant fungus with roots stretching back 65 million years
items.desc: Scientists have discovered a giant new fungus in China that grows up to 20 inches tall and weighs nearly five pounds, making it the largest known of its kind. Dubbed “D-rex,” its evolutionary lineage appears to have emerged shortly after the dinosaurs went extinct, raising intriguing questions about how that ancient catastrophe may have shaped its evolution.

items.title: Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch
items.desc: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia. Researchers found that older adults with a specific genetic profile had a 70% lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect. The discovery suggests that genetics could help explain why some people benefit while others do not.

items.title: This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans
items.desc: For nearly a century, people in distant parts of the world have reported a bizarre experience after eating certain wild mushrooms: seeing dozens or even hundreds of tiny, colorful humans moving through the real world. Now, scientists have identified a mushroom species, Lanmaoa asiatica, responsible for these extraordinary hallucinations in China and the Philippines.

items.title: Another Crash Landing for Brazil’s Economy?
items.desc: Brazil’s floating exchange rate, high foreign-exchange reserves, strong commodity exports, and debt denominated predominantly in its own currency reduce its exposure to a balance-of-payments crisis. Nonetheless, continued fiscal deterioration under President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will carry high domestic costs.

items.title: Europe’s Make-or-Break Moment Has Arrived
items.desc: US President Donald Trump has not only abandoned Ukraine and America’s European allies, but has increasingly sided with Russian President Vladimir Putin. To preserve their sovereignty, Europeans must remain united in the face of outside pressure, which in turn requires managing political threats from within their borders.

items.title: Middle Powers Can Lead on AI Safety
items.desc: With the United States showing no interest in regulating AI, middle powers have an opportunity to take the lead on governance. By banding together, these countries could condition market access on meeting a common set of safety requirements and explore joint investment in technical capacity.

items.title: Lula Killed the Donroe Doctrine
items.desc: In attempting to disentangle the United States from the rest of the world and retreat into a seemingly controllable hemispheric stronghold, Donald Trump's Latin America strategy had fared better than the rest of his foreign policy. But following a defeat for the far right in Brazil, his project now looks dead in the water.

items.title: The Wrong Way to Compare Economic Size
items.desc: At the European Central Bank’s annual research conference, Paul Krugman concluded that, when it comes to “weaponized interdependence,” the EU is more powerful than both the US and China. But his reliance on PPP-adjusted GDP as a way to smooth out the volatility of nominal exchange rates ignores the even greater swings in PPP data.

items.title: Public Control for a Purposeful Economy
items.desc: As more governments recognize the need for greater public control over economic outcomes, they must be careful to define the concept well. What ultimately matters is not ownership, but the state’s capacity to steer economic activity toward strategic objectives in the service of the common good.

items.title: Rethinking Sustainable Livelihoods From the Ground Up
items.desc: In regions where economic activity has long revolved around fossil-fuel extraction, ensuring a just transition requires developing alternative livelihoods that account for each community’s specific needs. Regional endowment funds could be a useful vehicle for funding these local initiatives.

items.title: The Specter of an AI-Driven Slowdown
items.desc: The rush to finance AI infrastructure is driving up borrowing costs just as governments grapple with mounting debt and persistent fiscal deficits. If the AI investment boom falters, falling valuations could choke off financing, with little room for fiscal and monetary policy to cushion the economic shock.

items.title: Is a Chinese Implosion Looming?
items.desc: If current trends continue, the Chinese state will find itself exposed to a political succession crisis, a weakening economy, and a lack of resources to exercise power domestically and project it externally. It would be a perfect storm, with far-reaching global repercussions.

items.title: PS Events: Reinventing Europe – Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala
items.desc: When we talk about "reinvention" we often overlook what works, noted WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala in her closing keynote. This is true of the global trading system, which has proven surprisingly resilient in recent years, and of the European economy, which might not have a tech giant to rival those in the US or China, but remains a global trade powerhouse and a leader in science and research. items.title: Who Pays the Fiscal Watchdogs?
items.desc: Civil-society oversight is the cheapest insurance in sovereign finance, because it enables independent scrutiny long before a default. But given that a borrowing government will never volunteer to fund the people who audit it, global decision-makers must do so using agreements for stolen-asset recovery and sovereign-debt treatments.

items.title: How to Help Left-Behind Regions
items.desc: Pouring public investment into poorer towns and cities might be politically beneficial, but the economic returns of indiscriminate largesse would be limited. A better approach would concentrate investment in areas with the potential to become high-productivity hubs, such as large peripheral cities.

items.title: The Agentic Information Economy
items.desc: An internet populated and run by AI agents will need not just reliable data but also a broader information ecology capable of questioning its own inputs and transmitting corrections where they are needed if information changes. But whether this will serve private interests or the public good remains to be seen.

items.title: A Competitive Europe Must Be Climate-Resilient
items.desc: Extreme weather and climate-related events caused €822 billion in economic losses across the European Union between 1980 and 2024, with a quarter of the losses occurring just in the last five years. The consequences for Europe’s competitiveness and economic security are clear—and so is the appropriate response.

items.title: Europe Must Prepare for the Worst
items.desc: Those seeking to weaken the EU’s supranational foundations are already preparing their radical schemes, like the “new deal for Europe” that Germany's Alternative für Deutschland recently presented in the European Parliament. The pro-EU camp must be prepared with new political strategies and institutional arrangements.
